subject: Runway surge characterization — evidence package and test methodology
messages:
From: Reed McAllister <reed@novagrid.com>
To: jonas_weber@redwood.ai
Cc: Aisha (Platform Eng) <aisha@novagrid.com>, NovaGrid Procurement <procurement@novagrid.com>
Date: Wed, 16 Jun 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: RFP Q: surge characterization and evidence for runway scenarios

Jonas —

Thanks for the quick intro last week. As part of our vendor evaluation we need a compact evidence package that demonstrates how Redwood handles short-duration surge events that exceed provisioned throughput (what we call "runway" spikes). Specifically we need:

- A short description of the test methodology you used to reproduce runway spikes (workload shaping, user mix, seed inputs)
- Key metrics you collect (latency quantiles, tail decomposition, error modes) and which ones you consider gating for production acceptance
- A representative data sample or CSV of requests/responses from a runway run (anonymized ok)
- Any automated fallback policies your platform used during the spike (model downgrade, regional fallback, queued requests)
- A summary of how caching (prefix/KV) and batching were instrumented during these runs

We have a 48-hour window to assemble materials for our procurement committee. Could you respond with an evidence packet and short notes?

-Reed
Procurement Lead, NovaGrid

From: jonas_weber@redwood.ai
To: Reed McAllister <reed@novagrid.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, hannah_schmitt@redwood.ai
Date: Thu, 17 Jun 2027 10:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: RFP Q: surge characterization and evidence for runway scenarios

Reed —

Appreciate the clarity. We're attaching a concise evidence packet and below is a high-level methodology summary you can share with the committee. Full lab notebooks and raw traces are included in the attached ZIP for your engineering reviewers.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Test type: synthetic mixed traffic with real-request seeds (customer telemetry representative of a 60/30/10 mix: short completions / long-form / embeddings).
- Surge profile: 30s ramp to 12x baseline QPS followed by a 90s plateau and then a 2min decay. We call this a "runway-quick" because of short duration but high amplitude.
- Acceptance criteria used: p99 latency under 2x baseline p99, p99.9 under 5x baseline p99, error rate increase < 0.5% absolute, and sustained throughput drop not exceeding 20% of baseline for >30s.

Methodology in detail:
1) Workload generation: we use a hybrid harness combining recorded production seeds (anonymized) and synthetic jitter. Seeds preserve token length distribution and model temperature used in production. Traffic is replayed across multiple client traces to preserve inter-arrival correlations.

2) Shaping & orchestration: runway spikes simulated with an open-loop generator that can push to target QPS with configurable ramp/plateau/decay phases. Multiple lanes emulate parallel tenants to exercise multi-tenant scheduler and KV-prefix cache contention.

3) Instrumentation & metrics: per-request timing (queue, batching wait, model inference, kernel-run), token-level reason codes (kv_cache_hit, cold_kv, quant_invocation), and resource counters (GPU util, memory, kernel latency). We report p50/p90/p99/p99.9/p99.99 and latency composition breakdowns (queue vs kernel vs serialization).

4) Cache & batching controls: prefix caching enabled in all runs, with explicit cache priming for long-lived sessions. Batch sizing is enforced by a latency SLO policy (max batching window 25ms for latency-sensitive lanes, 100ms for throughput lanes). We instrument adaptive batching and include logs of batch size distribution per-second.

5) Fallbacks and degradation: policy hierarchy = local replica fallback (model variant lower-precision) -> regional fallback -> queued requests with explicit client-backpressure signal. During runway-quick tests, we exercised model variant fallbacks (8-bit quantized variant) and observed an expected latency reduction at the cost of marginal coherence drop (we attach evaluation deltas).

Attachments included: runway_evidence_manifest.csv (summary rows for each run), runway_surge_playbook.pdf (step-by-step playbook + run parameters), trace_samples_202706.zip (sanitized traces and per-request timing).

If your reviewers need a sanitized per-token trace in CSV instead of the JSONL in the ZIP, tell us which fields you need and we can export.

Cheers,
Jonas Weber
Head of Sales Engineering, Redwood Inference
jonas_weber@redwood.ai

Jonas/Marissa —

Thanks for the packet. A couple of engineering clarifications before the committee meeting: 
- When you say "cache priming for long-lived sessions", do you simulate cold-starts for new sessions during the runway? We expect a mix of warmed and cold prefixes.
- For the model-variant fallback, what are the exact quantization profiles used and which layers (if any) are left in FP16 to preserve quality in degradations?
- Can you provide the CSV with the batch size distribution per-second for the plateau window of the runway-quick run (we need to plug this into our internal SLO model).

Appreciate the quick turnaround.

—Aisha
Platform Engineering, NovaGrid
From: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
To: Aisha (Platform Eng) <aisha@novagrid.com>, Reed McAllister <reed@novagrid.com>
Cc: jonas_weber@redwood.ai, hannah_schmitt@redwood.ai
Date: Fri, 18 Jun 2027 17:34:00 -0700
Subject: Re: RFP Q: surge characterization and evidence for runway scenarios

Aisha —

Quick answers and the requested CSV attached (attached filename: runway_plateau_batchdist.csv). Full notes: 

1) Cold/warm mix: runs include an explicit cold-injection step. For the runway-quick profile we used a 20% cold-session mix (randomized session IDs that bypass prefix cache) to emulate new sessions spiking. We then ran a subsequent priming pass to measure recovery time for cache hit-rate. Charts in the playbook show hit-rate vs time.

2) Quantization profiles & fallbacks: primary production model used a mixed-precision (FP16 kernels) path. Fallback variant is 8-bit symmetric quantization with selective FP16 passthrough on attention and final layer-norms (to avoid catastrophic divergence). The playbook contains microbenchmarks showing ROUGE/BLEU/embedding-cosine deltas per workload; typical degradation during fallback was within 1.5-3% for our long-form tests and <0.5% on short completions.

3) Batch distribution CSV: attached as requested. CSV columns: second_offset, qps, avg_batch_size, p50_batch_size, p90_batch_size, p99_batch_size. Sample row for plateau start included in the manifest.

If you want, we can schedule a 30-minute technical walkthrough with our runtime engineering lead to step through the ZIP traces and the playbook figures ahead of your procurement meeting. Available windows: Mon/Tue next week (PST mornings).

Best,
Marissa Cole
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
